catalog_quote: Doke 1925: 130: "ʗhũ: is an isolating language, in the construction of which most words are monosyllabic and word-position is the main feature. Musical "tone" on each syllable practically takes the place of stress as it is found in non-tone languages, and a change in tone may indicate an entire change in meaning." -- 136 (Length and Stress): "Stress, however, is not so important a subject. Since, to a great extent, the structure of the language is monosyllabic, tone rather than stress composes the sentence rhythm. However, in certain words where there are more syllables than one, it is found that a certain stress occurs on the syllable containing a long vowel; for instance, ǂˀá:xobo. This stress, naturally, it is unnecessary to indicate." -- 149-150: "My findings concur with those of H. Vedder at Gaub that there are five species of tone employed in ʗhũ: ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Chu: (Neitsas/Grootfontein !Xun) is a tone language with five tones (high, mid, low level, falling, rising; pp.149-150); stress is not distinctive and plays no rhythmic role; in polysyllabic words a non-contrastive stress falls on the syllable that contains a long vowel (example with initial long vowel stressed), predictable and therefore left unmarked.
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress is described only for 'certain words where there are more syllables than one' and tied to vowel length. Note the second first-hand source, Vedder 1910-11 p.15 (C1 Gaub dialect, file + vedder_pages/), gives a different picture: 'Der Stärkeakzent liegt entweder auf der ersten Silbe !gụru donnern, oder auf der zweiten Silbe, !gurụ Nagel an Fingern und Zehen, oder er liegt auf beiden Silben gleichmäßig, !gụrụ Köcher' (stress in disyllables on the 1st, the 2nd, or evenly on both syllables, lexically), while conceding that even stress 'wird leicht als Hochton wahrgenommen' and that separating dynamic stress from rising/falling tone is 'überaus schwierig' -- i.e. Vedder's 'Stärkeakzent' contrasts are probably tonal.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated lexical items in a phonetic outline); Doke explicitly says sentence rhythm is carried by tone, not stress. Most roots monosyllabic, so the stress remark concerns the minority of polysyllabic words.
new_statements.identity_note: Both first-hand sources describe lects that Heine & König (2015; classification reproduced in Heine & Honken 2010 Table 2) assign to the Central !Xun branch, which is exactly Glottolog's Central Ju [cent2300]: Doke 1925 worked at farm Neitsas/Nurugas, Grootfontein District (= dialect C2 'Neitsas'; Glottolog tags the article 'Grootfontein !Chu = Central Ju'); Vedder 1910-11 worked at farm Gaub near Tsumeb (= dialect C1 'Gaub'; Glottolog 5.1's MED for cent2300). Doke himself notes Vedder's Gaub speakers 'spoke a distinct dialect, though one undoubtedly belonging to the same tribe'. Caution: Amanda Miller's 'Mangetti Dune !Xung' phonetic work is NOT Central Ju (Miller 2013 groups it with Ekoka !Xun, i.e. North-Central Ju kung1261 / Kavango !Xun), even though Glottolog files Miller 2011 under Central Ju because it cites Grootfontein !Xung click data; Tsintsabis !Xun (W3) is likewise Northwestern, not Central.

sources.citation: Miller, Amanda. 2013. Northern Khoesan: phonetics and phonology. In Rainer Vossen (ed.), The Khoesan Languages, pp.44-49 (approx.). London: Routledge.
sources.note: Focuses on Ju|'hoan; mentions Central Ju 'Grootfontein !Xung' only for its retroflex click (Miller-Ockhuizen & Sands 1999, 2000); root tone patterns for Ju|'hoan; nothing on stress for any !Xun variety.
